claimVerdicts.note: Matches the abstract of 212 (p1), including the authors' statement that the observational design 'precludes the examination of causal relationships'; 36 team-seasons, 16 elite teams in top European leagues.
Abstract gives '18%, 45% and 72% of turnarounds with > 85% runs for 3, 5 and 7-turnarounds'; individual thresholds are confirmed on p4.

Abstract of 269 states central days exceeded post and pre-match days and that 'MD-2 was the day that required the least stimuli (p < 0.05)'; p7 attributes this to 'the peculiarity of the planning proposal used by the team'.
Practical applications and limitations on p8 say this, including that generalisation depends 'above all, on the training philosophy established by staff'.

The abstract (p2) lists MD-4, MD-3 and MD+1 as the highest training WCS, and the conclusion (p12, page 11 in the journal) says -4MD/-3MD 'usually reported greater demands than -2MD, -1MD, or +1MD'. The claim reports this internal inconsistency accurately.
Abstract conclusion says WCS drills 'may be useful'. The claim correctly calls it a suggestion.
Abstract and p2 confirm a reserve squad of a Spanish La Liga club, with more match time linked to higher accumulated weekly load for most variables.
The practical applications on p9 say 'the MD-1, MD and MD+1 sessions could be the most appropriate sessions to try to compensate'. This is an untested suggestion, as the claim says.
p2 says 'the present study only analysed training weeks where players had six days between successive matches'.
p8 discussion and limitations match. 21 players, Iranian Premier League, full season.
p12 says teams refrain on MD+1/MD+2, and the low-participation recommendation cites ref 47. The p4 methods confirm responses covered only players with more significant involvement.

statementIssues.note: 'Links it to fewer match hamstring injuries' is slightly stronger than the source. 212 reports zero injuries at D-2 with overlapping CIs and no pooled difference. These caveats appear in actions[2], guardrails[1] and evidenceTension, but not in the bottom line itself.

'So note travel days in the record' is generic advice. It is not labelled as professional judgment, although the cited claims only show that travel may limit recovery and that no evidence-based travel management exists.
Calling the collegiate source an off-season case series elsewhere (actions[4]) slightly simplifies it: one of the seven injuries (Case 6) occurred preseason. This does not change the decision.

tierNote: Limited is appropriate. The evidence is mostly single-club professional soccer, descriptive or observational, and conflicts on D-2 near-maximal speed. Nothing addresses collegiate rosters, travel or validated progress/hold/adjust criteria. recommendedDirection is null, and the near-maximal speed timing is presented as two documented options rather than a recommendation.
usefulnessNote: The brief is organised by athlete group (recently played, low-minute, modified participation) and exposure type, which matches the request. It is honest about the D-2 tension and keeps medical plans controlling. It labels its professional judgment and clearly lists the gaps: no validated progress/hold/adjust rules, travel or conditioning for modified athletes. It is dense for a two-minute read, and conditioning allocation and travel get little concrete support.
suggestedDrafterFixes: When the bottom line cites an observational association whose pooled analysis is null or whose CIs overlap, put a short qualifier in the bottom line itself rather than only in guardrails.
Label any procedural advice that is not drawn from a claim (for example 'note travel days') as professional judgment, consistent with the actions.
Check case-series timing descriptors (off-season vs preseason) against each case before summarising them.
